questions.prompt: Which word is an adjective in “The narrow bridge was closed”?
explanations: Narrow describes what kind of bridge it is, so it functions as an adjective.
Bridge names a thing, so it is a noun rather than an adjective.
Closed is a past participle functioning as part of the passive verb phrase was closed.
questions.grammar_rule: An adjective describes a noun; here narrow modifies bridge.
questions.example_sentence: The quiet room felt peaceful.

questions.prompt: In “The children laughed loudly,” what part of speech is “loudly”?
explanations: An adjective modifies a noun, but loudly modifies the action laughed.
Loudly describes how the children laughed, making it an adverb of manner.
A noun names a person, place, thing or idea; loudly does not name one.
questions.grammar_rule: An adverb can describe how an action occurs.
questions.example_sentence: The audience clapped enthusiastically.

questions.prompt: In “Maya carefully packed her bag,” which word is a verb?
explanations: “Carefully” describes how Maya packed; it is an adverb, not the action verb.
“packed” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Packed expresses the action Maya performed.
“Bag” names the object packed; it is a noun, not a verb.
questions.grammar_rule: Packed expresses the action Maya performed.
questions.example_sentence: Maya packed her bag before school.

questions.prompt: Which word is a conjunction in “I called, but nobody answered”?
explanations: “Called” expresses an action; it is a verb rather than a joining word.
“but” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. But joins two clauses and signals a contrast.
“Nobody” refers to a person in an indefinite way; it is a pronoun, not a conjunction.
questions.grammar_rule: But joins two clauses and signals a contrast.
questions.example_sentence: I wanted to go, but I was tired.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct plural: “Three ___ crossed the field.”
explanations: Gooses is not the standard plural of goose.
Goose is singular, but three requires a plural noun.
Geese is the irregular plural of goose, so it agrees with three.
questions.grammar_rule: Goose has the irregular plural geese.
questions.example_sentence: Two mice hid behind the box.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an uncountable noun naturally?
explanations: Some advice correctly treats advice as an uncountable noun.
An advice incorrectly uses an indefinite article with an uncountable noun.
Two advices incorrectly makes advice countable; say two pieces of advice.
questions.grammar_rule: Advice is normally uncountable in standard English.
questions.example_sentence: She gave me useful information.

questions.prompt: One analysis, two _____.
explanations: “analyses” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. The plural of analysis is analyses.
“Analysises” adds an incorrect plural ending to the noun analysis.
“Analysis” is singular and cannot follow “two” in this context.
questions.grammar_rule: The plural of analysis is analyses.
questions.example_sentence: One analysis, two analyses.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the possessive form correctly?
explanations: “Childrens” omits the apostrophe required to indicate possession.
“The children’s toys are outside.” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Children is already plural; add apostrophe s for its possessive.
“Childrens’” wrongly treats childrens as a regular plural; the plural is children.
questions.grammar_rule: Children is already plural; add apostrophe s for its possessive.
questions.example_sentence: The student's notebook is on the desk.

questions.prompt: Lena and I made the cake. Mum thanked ___.
explanations: We is a subject pronoun, not the object of thanked.
Us is the object pronoun referring to Lena and the speaker.
Ours is a possessive pronoun, which does not work as the object here.
questions.grammar_rule: Use an object pronoun after a transitive verb.
questions.example_sentence: The teacher helped them.

questions.prompt: This scarf belongs to Ravi. It is ___.
explanations: Him is an object pronoun and does not indicate possession by itself.
His is a possessive pronoun that stands alone after is.
He is a subject pronoun, so it cannot express ownership here.
questions.grammar_rule: Use a possessive pronoun to replace a possessed noun phrase.
questions.example_sentence: That notebook is hers.

questions.prompt: The blue jacket is _____.
explanations: “My” is a possessive determiner and requires a following noun such as jacket.
“Me” is an object pronoun, not a possessive form that can stand alone.
“mine” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Mine is a possessive pronoun that stands without a following noun.
questions.grammar_rule: Mine is a possessive pronoun that stands without a following noun.
questions.example_sentence: The blue jacket is mine.

questions.prompt: The twins made the cake _____.
explanations: “themselves” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. The reflexive pronoun for plural the twins is themselves.
“Theirselves” is not the standard English reflexive form for they.
“Themself” does not agree with the plural subject “the twins” in this standard usage.
questions.grammar_rule: The reflexive pronoun for plural the twins is themselves.
questions.example_sentence: The twins made the cake themselves.

questions.prompt: Nila saw ___ owl sitting on the wall.
explanations: A precedes consonant sounds, but owl begins with a vowel sound.
The would suggest a particular owl already identified, which this first mention does not establish.
An correctly introduces one unspecified owl whose name begins with a vowel sound.
questions.grammar_rule: Use an before a vowel sound when mentioning one indefinite countable noun.
questions.example_sentence: He bought an umbrella.

questions.prompt: ___ water in this bottle is warm, but the water in that bottle is cold.
explanations: The specifies the water in this particular bottle.
A cannot directly modify the uncountable noun water in this use.
An also cannot directly modify the uncountable noun water here.
questions.grammar_rule: The identifies a specific portion of an uncountable substance.
questions.example_sentence: The rice on this plate is spicy.

questions.prompt: I saw a dog yesterday. _____ dog followed me home.
explanations: “A” introduces an unspecified dog; the second mention refers to the known dog.
“An” cannot precede the consonant sound in “dog” and does not mark known reference.
“The” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Use the for a dog already introduced in the context.
questions.grammar_rule: Use the for a dog already introduced in the context.
questions.example_sentence: I saw a dog yesterday. The dog followed me home.

questions.prompt: There is _____ milk left; we need to buy more.
explanations: “Few” quantifies plural countable nouns, not uncountable milk.
“A few” also requires a plural countable noun rather than milk.
“little” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Little is used with uncountable milk to indicate a small amount.
questions.grammar_rule: Little is used with uncountable milk to indicate a small amount.
questions.example_sentence: There is little milk left; we need to buy more.

questions.prompt: Of the four routes, this is the ___.
explanations: Short is a positive adjective and does not express the highest degree.
Shorter is comparative, usually contrasting two items, not identifying one among four.
Shortest is the superlative identifying the minimum length among four routes.
questions.grammar_rule: Use the superlative for one member compared with three or more.
questions.example_sentence: This is the tallest building in our street.

questions.prompt: The new table is ___ than the old one.
explanations: Wide lacks the comparative marking required with than.
Wider correctly compares the width of the two tables.
Widest is a superlative, not the comparative required with than.
questions.grammar_rule: Use the comparative degree with than to compare two things.
questions.example_sentence: This road is narrower than that road.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an adjective rather than an adverb?
explanations: “The soup tastes delicious.” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Delicious describes the subject soup after the linking verb tastes.
“Beautifully” modifies sings, a verb; it is an adverb.
“Slowly” modifies walked, a verb; it is an adverb.
questions.grammar_rule: Delicious describes the subject soup after the linking verb tastes.
questions.example_sentence: She wore a beautiful dress.

questions.prompt: It was _____ interesting film that we watched it twice.
explanations: “So” requires an adjective plus a separate structure, not “so interesting film.”
“such an” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Such an is used before an adjective plus singular countable noun.
“Such” needs the indefinite article before singular countable “film”: such an interesting film.
questions.grammar_rule: Such an is used before an adjective plus singular countable noun.
questions.example_sentence: It was such an interesting film that we watched it twice.

questions.prompt: Please speak ___ so everyone can hear you clearly.
explanations: Slowly describes the manner of speaking and modifies the verb.
Slow is generally an adjective here; slowly is the expected adverb form for this instruction.
Slowness is a noun and cannot naturally describe how to speak in this sentence.
questions.grammar_rule: An adverb of manner commonly modifies the verb speak.
questions.example_sentence: He answered politely.

questions.prompt: She has ___ finished the report; it is ready to send.
explanations: Yet is typically used in negatives and questions, not here before finished in an affirmative statement.
Already naturally signals the report is completed by now.
Still before finished does not convey completed action in this construction.
questions.grammar_rule: Already can indicate an action has been completed before now.
questions.example_sentence: We have already eaten lunch.

questions.prompt: Which sentence places the frequency adverb naturally?
explanations: With the verb be, “always” normally follows “is”; “she always is” is marked emphasis, not the neutral placement requested.
“She is always late.” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Frequency adverbs usually follow the verb be.
This arrangement lacks the normal subject–verb order of an English declarative sentence.
questions.grammar_rule: Frequency adverbs usually follow the verb be.
questions.example_sentence: He usually walks to school.

questions.prompt: He speaks English _____.
explanations: “Fluent” is an adjective, but the sentence needs an adverb modifying speaks.
“fluently” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Fluently is the adverb that describes how he speaks.
“Fluency” is a noun and cannot directly modify “speaks” in this sentence.
questions.grammar_rule: Fluently is the adverb that describes how he speaks.
questions.example_sentence: He speaks English fluently.

questions.prompt: The picture hangs ___ the fireplace.
explanations: Under indicates a lower position, contradicting the intended location.
Above places the picture higher than the fireplace.
Between requires two reference points, but only one fireplace is mentioned.
questions.grammar_rule: Above means at a higher position without requiring contact.
questions.example_sentence: The clock hangs above the doorway.

questions.prompt: The train leaves ___ 6:15 a.m.
explanations: At is the usual preposition before an exact time.
On is normally used with named days and dates, not clock times alone.
In is generally used for months, years or longer periods, not 6:15 a.m.
questions.grammar_rule: Use at with precise clock times.
questions.example_sentence: Our class starts at nine.

questions.prompt: The picture hangs _____ the fireplace.
explanations: “above” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Above indicates a higher position without requiring contact.
“Through” indicates movement within an opening or passage, not a static vertical position.
“During” expresses time, not the spatial position of the picture.
questions.grammar_rule: Above indicates a higher position without requiring contact.
questions.example_sentence: The picture hangs above the fireplace.

questions.prompt: We walked _____ the tunnel to reach the station.
explanations: “Across” indicates crossing a surface or area rather than moving inside the tunnel.
“through” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Through describes movement inside a tunnel from one end to the other.
“Beside” means next to the tunnel, not passing within it.
questions.grammar_rule: Through describes movement inside a tunnel from one end to the other.
questions.example_sentence: We walked through the tunnel to reach the station.

questions.prompt: We stayed indoors ___ the storm was severe.
explanations: Although expresses contrast, not the stated reason for staying indoors.
Unless introduces a condition meaning if not, which does not express the reason here.
Because explains that the severe storm caused the decision to stay indoors.
questions.grammar_rule: Because introduces a reason for the main action.
questions.example_sentence: We left early because it was getting dark.

questions.prompt: ___ she was nervous, Mira delivered a confident speech.
explanations: Although captures the contrast between nervousness and confident delivery.
Because indicates cause, but being nervous does not explain a confident performance in this contrast.
So is not used to introduce this subordinate clause before the main clause.
questions.grammar_rule: Although introduces a concessive clause contrasting with the main clause.
questions.example_sentence: Although it rained, the match continued.

questions.prompt: You may borrow the book _____ you return it tomorrow.
explanations: “provided that” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Provided that introduces a condition for permission.
“Despite” takes a noun or -ing phrase, not the finite clause used here without restructuring.
“Whereas” expresses contrast rather than a condition attached to borrowing.
questions.grammar_rule: Provided that introduces a condition for permission.
questions.example_sentence: You may borrow the book provided that you return it tomorrow.

questions.prompt: I brought a charger _____ my phone might run out of power.
explanations: “in case” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. In case introduces a precaution taken against a possibility.
“So that not” is an ungrammatical way to express this precautionary purpose.
“Unless” means except if, not a precaution against a possible event.
questions.grammar_rule: In case introduces a precaution taken against a possibility.
questions.example_sentence: I brought a charger in case my phone might run out of power.

questions.prompt: Every evening, Dev ___ a short walk after dinner.
explanations: Take lacks the required -s for the singular subject Dev.
Takes agrees with Dev in the simple present for a habit.
Taking cannot serve as the finite main verb without an auxiliary.
questions.grammar_rule: Simple-present third-person singular subjects take -s or -es.
questions.example_sentence: She reads before bed.

questions.prompt: Look! The children ___ a kite in the park.
explanations: Are flying describes the action happening right now, as signaled by Look.
Fly describes a general habit, rather than this ongoing event.
Have flown describes a completed or relevant past experience, not the action unfolding now.
questions.grammar_rule: Use the present continuous for an action happening at this moment.
questions.example_sentence: The dog is sleeping now.

questions.prompt: I _____ this teacher for five years.
explanations: “have known” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Present perfect describes a state continuing from the past to now.
“Am knowing” uses a progressive form with the stative verb know in this meaning.
“Know since” lacks the present-perfect auxiliary needed for the continuing period.
questions.grammar_rule: Present perfect describes a state continuing from the past to now.
questions.example_sentence: I have known this teacher for five years.

questions.prompt: By noon, I _____ three emails today.
explanations: “have already sent” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Present perfect connects earlier actions with the unfinished period today.
“Had already send” uses the base form after had instead of the past participle sent.
“Am already send” lacks the -ing participle and is not a valid continuous construction.
questions.grammar_rule: Present perfect connects earlier actions with the unfinished period today.
questions.example_sentence: By noon, I have already sent three emails today.

questions.prompt: Yesterday, I ___ my wallet on the bus.
explanations: Lose is present-tense base form and does not match yesterday.
Lost is the past form of lose and matches yesterday.
Have lost is present perfect, normally not paired with a definite past time such as yesterday.
questions.grammar_rule: Use the simple past for a completed event at a specified past time.
questions.example_sentence: We visited the museum yesterday.

questions.prompt: By the time we reached the cinema, the film ___.
explanations: Starts is present tense, unlike the two past events.
Has started is present perfect, not the expected tense for the earlier of two past events.
Had started marks the film beginning before we reached the cinema.
questions.grammar_rule: Use past perfect for a past action completed before another past event.
questions.example_sentence: The bus had left before we arrived.

questions.prompt: When I reached the station, the train _____.
explanations: “Has left” connects a past event to the present instead of placing departure before a past arrival.
“had left” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Past perfect places the departure before my arrival.
“Leaves” is present simple and does not mark departure before the past arrival.
questions.grammar_rule: Past perfect places the departure before my arrival.
questions.example_sentence: When I reached the station, the train had left.

questions.prompt: She _____ in Madrid in 2019.
explanations: “Has lived” conflicts with the completed past time reference “in 2019” for this intended event.
“lived” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. A finished time reference like in 2019 calls for past simple.
“Had living” is not a grammatical past-perfect construction.
questions.grammar_rule: A finished time reference like in 2019 calls for past simple.
questions.example_sentence: She lived in Madrid in 2019.

questions.prompt: Look at those dark clouds. It ___ rain soon.
explanations: Is going to expresses a prediction supported by the visible clouds.
Was going to places the intention or prediction in the past.
Has rain is not a grammatical verb phrase in this context.
questions.grammar_rule: Be going to is common for predictions based on present evidence.
questions.example_sentence: The sky is black; it is going to storm.

questions.prompt: The meeting ___ at 10 a.m. tomorrow, according to the official schedule.
explanations: Is starting to requires a following verb phrase and does not complete the sentence naturally.
Starts is appropriate for an official scheduled event in the future.
Had started is past perfect and cannot describe tomorrow’s scheduled meeting.
questions.grammar_rule: The simple present can describe fixed future timetables.
questions.example_sentence: The flight departs at seven tomorrow.

questions.prompt: Our flight _____ at 6:30 tomorrow morning.
explanations: “Leave” lacks third-person singular agreement with the subject “our flight.”
“leaves” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Simple present can express a fixed timetable.
“Left” describes a past departure, not the scheduled departure tomorrow.
questions.grammar_rule: Simple present can express a fixed timetable.
questions.example_sentence: Our flight leaves at 6:30 tomorrow morning.

questions.prompt: By this time next week, we _____ the training.
explanations: “will have completed” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Future perfect marks completion before a future reference point.
“Will completing” omits the required auxiliary be or have and is ungrammatical.
“Have complete” uses a base verb rather than the past participle completed.
questions.grammar_rule: Future perfect marks completion before a future reference point.
questions.example_sentence: By this time next week, we will have completed the training.

questions.prompt: While my brother was cooking, I ___ the table.
explanations: Set is also the simple past of set and suits this past narrative.
Am setting is present continuous and conflicts with the established past-time frame.
Will set places the event in the future, not alongside past cooking.
questions.grammar_rule: Use a past form for a simultaneous event located in a past narrative.
questions.example_sentence: While I was reading, Dad made tea.

questions.prompt: She said she ___ the documents the previous day.
explanations: Submits is simple present, which does not match the past reporting frame and previous day.
Had submitted locates the submission before she spoke.
Will submit refers to a future submission rather than a completed past action.
questions.grammar_rule: Reported speech often uses past perfect for an action earlier than a past reporting time.
questions.example_sentence: He said he had arrived the day before.

questions.prompt: He opened the door and _____ inside.
explanations: “walked” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Two sequential completed past actions take past simple.
“Walks yesterday” combines present-tense agreement with an explicit past-time word.
“Has walked then” does not fit the completed sequence marked by opened and then.
questions.grammar_rule: Two sequential completed past actions take past simple.
questions.example_sentence: He opened the door and walked inside.

questions.prompt: If I finish early, I _____ you.
explanations: “Called yesterday” is past tense; the future consequence of a possible condition needs future meaning.
“will call” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. A real future condition uses present simple in the if-clause and will in the main clause.
“Had called” marks an earlier past event, not the future result of finishing early.
questions.grammar_rule: A real future condition uses present simple in the if-clause and will in the main clause.
questions.example_sentence: If I finish early, I will call you.

questions.prompt: Each of the players ___ a numbered shirt.
explanations: Have is plural agreement and does not match each as the subject head.
Has correctly agrees with the singular word each.
Are having uses plural agreement and is not appropriate for possession in this context.
questions.grammar_rule: Each is singular and takes singular verb agreement in formal standard English.
questions.example_sentence: Each student has a desk.

questions.prompt: The list of supplies ___ on the office wall.
explanations: Is agrees with the singular head noun list.
Are incorrectly agrees with supplies inside the prepositional phrase rather than list.
Be cannot serve as the finite present-tense verb in this sentence.
questions.grammar_rule: The head noun list is singular even when its modifier mentions plural supplies.
questions.example_sentence: The box of pencils is on the shelf.

questions.prompt: Neither the teacher nor the students _____ ready.
explanations: “Is” is singular, but the nearer coordinated subject students is plural.
“are” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. With neither/nor, the plural nearest subject students takes are.
“Be” is the base verb and does not agree with the present-tense subject here.
questions.grammar_rule: With neither/nor, the plural nearest subject students takes are.
questions.example_sentence: Neither the teacher nor the students are ready.

questions.prompt: Each of these reports _____ a summary.
explanations: “Have” is plural agreement; each is singular in this construction.
“has” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Each takes a singular verb in standard formal English.
“Having” is a non-finite participle and cannot serve as the main finite verb alone.
questions.grammar_rule: Each takes a singular verb in standard formal English.
questions.example_sentence: Each of these reports has a summary.

questions.prompt: You ___ wear a helmet on this construction site; it is mandatory.
explanations: Might expresses possibility, not a compulsory site rule.
Must correctly conveys the mandatory safety requirement.
Could expresses possibility or ability, not a requirement.
questions.grammar_rule: Must expresses strong obligation or a rule.
questions.example_sentence: Passengers must fasten their seat belts.

questions.prompt: When she was six, she ___ already swim across the pool.
explanations: Can normally expresses present ability rather than past ability at age six.
Will describes future prediction or willingness, not past ability.
Could correctly expresses the ability she had when she was six.
questions.grammar_rule: Could expresses general ability in the past.
questions.example_sentence: At five, he could read simple stories.

questions.prompt: You _____ have bought bread; we already had plenty.
explanations: “needn’t” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Needn’t have expresses that a completed action was unnecessary.
“Mustn’t have bought” generally signals a prohibition or different inference, not an unnecessary completed purchase.
“Can’t have bought” expresses an inference that the purchase did not happen, rather than its needless nature.
questions.grammar_rule: Needn’t have expresses that a completed action was unnecessary.
questions.example_sentence: You needn’t have bought bread; we already had plenty.

questions.prompt: She _____ be at home; the lights are on and her car is outside.
explanations: “must” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Must expresses a strong deduction based on present evidence.
“Must not” asserts prohibition or strong negative expectation, opposite to the evidence-based deduction.
“Should have” refers to an expected past situation and does not directly infer present location.
questions.grammar_rule: Must expresses a strong deduction based on present evidence.
questions.example_sentence: She must be at home; the lights are on and her car is outside.

questions.prompt: ___ your sister finished her homework yet?
explanations: Has agrees with the singular subject your sister and forms the present perfect.
Have does not agree with the singular subject your sister.
Does would require finish, not the past participle finished, in a simple-present question.
questions.grammar_rule: Present perfect questions use has with a third-person singular subject.
questions.example_sentence: Has Arjun called you yet?

questions.prompt: Which sentence is a grammatical question?
explanations: Where you are going retains statement word order and is not the standard direct-question pattern.
Where are you going correctly inverts are and you.
Where going you are misorders the auxiliary and present participle.
questions.grammar_rule: Most direct questions place the auxiliary before the subject.
questions.example_sentence: What is she doing?

questions.prompt: She doesn’t _____ coffee.
explanations: “Drinks” incorrectly retains the third-person ending after the auxiliary doesn’t.
“Drinking” is a participle; after doesn’t the base form drink is required.
“drink” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. After doesn’t, use the base form of the main verb.
questions.grammar_rule: After doesn’t, use the base form of the main verb.
questions.example_sentence: She doesn’t drink coffee.

questions.prompt: Nobody called, _____?
explanations: “did they” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. A negative-meaning statement takes a positive question tag.
“Didn’t they” repeats a negative tag after the negative-meaning nobody; use a positive tag.
“Was it” mismatches both the past lexical verb called and the person-reference in nobody.
questions.grammar_rule: A negative-meaning statement takes a positive question tag.
questions.example_sentence: Nobody called, did they?

questions.prompt: Which option is a complete sentence?
explanations: Because the door was locked is a dependent clause without a main clause.
Across the empty street is a prepositional phrase, not a complete clause.
The visitors waited outside contains a subject and a finite verb and expresses a complete thought.
questions.grammar_rule: An independent clause can stand alone as a complete sentence.
questions.example_sentence: The rain stopped suddenly.

questions.prompt: Choose the correctly combined sentence.
options: Although it was late, we continued working.
Although it was late, but we continued working.
explanations: Although introduces the concession and the main clause follows naturally.
Using although and but together here duplicates the contrast marker.
This option combines a fragment with an unnecessary but and lacks a clear main-clause subject.
questions.grammar_rule: Do not normally combine although and but to link the same two clauses.
questions.example_sentence: Although she was tired, she smiled.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence with parallel structure.
options: She likes reading, to swim, and cycling.
She likes reading, swimming, and cycling.
She likes read, swimming, and cycling.
explanations: “To swim” breaks the coordinated -ing pattern established by reading and cycling.
“She likes reading, swimming, and cycling.” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Parallel list items use matching -ing forms.
“Read” breaks the consistent parallel gerund sequence used for the listed activities.
questions.grammar_rule: Parallel list items use matching -ing forms.
questions.example_sentence: She enjoys reading, writing, and drawing.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly places the modifier?
options: Walking home, the rain soaked Maya.
Walking home, Maya got soaked by rain.
The rain walking home soaked Maya.
explanations: The opening modifier appears to describe the rain as walking home, creating a dangling modifier.
“Walking home, Maya got soaked by rain.” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. The introductory modifier Walking home correctly describes Maya.
This sentence incorrectly assigns walking home to rain and gives an unnatural clause structure.
questions.grammar_rule: The introductory modifier Walking home correctly describes Maya.
questions.example_sentence: Walking to school, I saw a rainbow.

questions.prompt: Choose the passive form of “The chef prepared the meal.”
options: The meal was prepared by the chef.
The chef was prepared the meal.
explanations: This changes the roles and wrongly says the meal prepares a person.
Was prepared correctly makes the meal the receiver of the action in the past.
The chef was prepared the meal has an incorrect passive structure and retains the active object.
questions.grammar_rule: A past passive clause uses was/were plus a past participle.
questions.example_sentence: The window was repaired yesterday.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is in the present continuous passive?
options: The bridge is being repaired today.
explanations: Repairs is active present-tense form and lacks the passive auxiliary.
Has repairing is not a grammatical tense or voice construction.
Is being repaired correctly describes work being done to the bridge now.
questions.grammar_rule: Present continuous passive uses am/is/are being plus past participle.
questions.example_sentence: The hall is being cleaned now.

questions.prompt: The invitations _____ tomorrow.
explanations: “Will send” is active and would require a sender subject; invitations receive the action.
“will be sent” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Future passive is will be plus past participle.
“Will be sending by” is incomplete and misforms the future passive.
questions.grammar_rule: Future passive is will be plus past participle.
questions.example_sentence: The invitations will be sent tomorrow.

questions.prompt: The documents should _____ before noon.
explanations: “be signed” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. A passive after should uses be plus past participle.
“Should signed” omits be after the modal for passive voice.
“Be signing” gives an ongoing active-style participle rather than required passive signed.
questions.grammar_rule: A passive after should uses be plus past participle.
questions.example_sentence: The documents should be signed before noon.

questions.prompt: Direct speech: Arun said, “I am tired.” Choose a natural past-time report.
options: Arun said that he was tired.
Arun said that I am tired.
Arun said that he will tired.
explanations: He was tired correctly reports Arun’s own state from a past viewpoint.
I changes the referent to the reporting speaker and does not correctly represent Arun.
Will tired is ungrammatical; will requires a base verb such as be.
questions.grammar_rule: In past reported speech, pronouns and tenses may shift with the viewpoint.
questions.example_sentence: Nina said that she was ready.

questions.prompt: Direct speech: “Where do you live?” she asked me. Choose the report.
options: She asked me where did I live.
She asked me where I lived.
She asked me where do I live.
explanations: Where did I live incorrectly keeps direct-question inversion in reported speech.
Where I lived uses the expected statement order and past reporting viewpoint.
Where do I live keeps direct question word order and the wrong speaker perspective.
questions.grammar_rule: Reported wh-questions use statement word order rather than inversion.
questions.example_sentence: He asked where the shop was.

questions.prompt: She said, “Please sit down.” Choose the reported request.
options: She asked me to sit down.
explanations: “She asked me to sit down.” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Asked plus object plus to-infinitive reports a polite request.
“Said me” is not the correct verb pattern for reporting a request.
“Asked that sit down” lacks a grammatical subject or infinitive to report the request.
questions.grammar_rule: Asked plus object plus to-infinitive reports a polite request.
questions.example_sentence: She asked us to sit down.

questions.prompt: “I will call tomorrow,” he said. Reporting later, choose the correct sentence.
options: He said he would call the next day.
He said he will called yesterday.
He said he would called tomorrow yesterday.
explanations: “He said he would call the next day.” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Will typically backshifts to would and tomorrow becomes the next day.
“Will called” is an impossible auxiliary-plus-past form and shifts the time reference incorrectly.
“Would called” needs the base verb call; the repeated time words are contradictory.
questions.grammar_rule: Will typically backshifts to would and tomorrow becomes the next day.
questions.example_sentence: He said he would call the next day.

questions.prompt: If I had studied harder, I ___ the exam.
explanations: Will pass expresses a real future possibility, not an unreal past result.
Would pass is associated with hypothetical present/future results, not this completed past exam.
Would have passed correctly expresses the hypothetical past result.
questions.grammar_rule: Third conditional expresses unreal past conditions and results.
questions.example_sentence: If she had left early, she would have caught the bus.

questions.prompt: If water reaches 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure, it ___.
explanations: Boils expresses the general result under the stated pressure condition.
Boiled places a general fact in the past without a past-time frame.
Would boil makes the scientifically stated regular result hypothetical rather than general.
questions.grammar_rule: Zero conditional states general truths using present-tense clauses.
questions.example_sentence: If ice gets warm enough, it melts.

questions.prompt: If she had studied, she _____ the exam.
explanations: “would have passed” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. The third conditional uses would have plus past participle for an unreal past result.
“Will pass yesterday” mixes future tense with past-time reference and fails the unreal past condition.
“Passes already” is present simple and cannot express the hypothetical past result.
questions.grammar_rule: The third conditional uses would have plus past participle for an unreal past result.
questions.example_sentence: If she had studied, she would have passed the exam.

questions.prompt: I wish I _____ how to play the piano.
explanations: “Know” uses present indicative where “wish” expresses an unreal present state.
“knew” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Wish plus past simple expresses an unreal present desire.
“Have knew” combines have with the wrong participle; knew is past tense, not known.
questions.grammar_rule: Wish plus past simple expresses an unreal present desire.
questions.example_sentence: I wish I knew how to play the piano.

questions.prompt: The artist ___ painted this mural lives nearby.
explanations: Which normally refers to things, not the person artist in this defining relative clause.
Who refers to the artist and acts as subject of painted.
Whose marks possession and would need a following noun in this structure.
questions.grammar_rule: Who is a subject relative pronoun referring to a person.
questions.example_sentence: The nurse who helped me was kind.

questions.prompt: This is the book ___ cover was designed by my sister.
explanations: Who refers to people and cannot express the book’s ownership of its cover here.
Which alone cannot modify cover to express possession; whose is required.
Whose correctly links the book to its cover.
questions.grammar_rule: Whose can show possession with people and things in relative clauses.
questions.example_sentence: We visited a house whose windows faced the sea.

questions.prompt: The café _____ we met has closed.
explanations: “where” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Where introduces a relative clause referring to a place.
“Who” refers to a person, whereas the relative clause identifies a place.
“Whose” introduces possession and cannot replace the locative relative where here.
questions.grammar_rule: Where introduces a relative clause referring to a place.
questions.example_sentence: The café where we met has closed.

questions.prompt: My uncle, _____ lives in Rome, is visiting us.
explanations: “That” is not normally used to introduce this non-defining relative clause after commas.
“who” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Who correctly introduces a nonrestrictive relative clause about a person.
“What” is not a personal relative pronoun referring back to uncle.
questions.grammar_rule: Who correctly introduces a nonrestrictive relative clause about a person.
questions.example_sentence: My uncle, who lives in Rome, is visiting us.

questions.prompt: They avoided ___ during the thunderstorm.
explanations: Driving is the gerund required after avoided.
Drive is a bare infinitive and does not follow avoided here.
To drive is an infinitive, whereas avoid takes the -ing form.
questions.grammar_rule: Avoid is normally followed by a gerund (-ing form).
questions.example_sentence: We avoid eating too late.

questions.prompt: She decided ___ for the scholarship.
explanations: Applying is a gerund and is not the usual direct complement of decided.
To apply is the infinitive complement required by decided.
Apply is a bare infinitive, which is not licensed by decided.
questions.grammar_rule: Decide is usually followed by a to-infinitive.
questions.example_sentence: He decided to learn French.

questions.prompt: She is interested in _____ French.
explanations: “Learn” is a bare infinitive; interested in requires a noun or -ing form.
“learning” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. After a preposition such as in, use the -ing form.
“To learn” is an infinitive; “in” is a preposition and normally takes learning here.
questions.grammar_rule: After a preposition such as in, use the -ing form.
questions.example_sentence: She is interested in learning French.

questions.prompt: He stopped _____ because he felt tired.
explanations: “Stopped to run” means paused another activity in order to run, not ceased running.
“running” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Stopped running means he ended the ongoing activity.
“Stopped run” uses an incorrect verb pattern; stop takes running for cessation.
questions.grammar_rule: Stopped running means he ended the ongoing activity.
questions.example_sentence: He stopped running because he felt tired.

questions.prompt: Which sentence has correct capitalization?
explanations: The first word we must begin with a capital letter.
Monday is a day name and must start with a capital letter.
Both We and Monday use the required capitalization.
questions.grammar_rule: Capitalize the first word of a sentence and names of days.
questions.example_sentence: They arrived on Friday.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence punctuated as a direct question.
explanations: The question mark correctly marks the direct question.
A period does not normally mark a direct question like this.
A comma cannot serve as the closing punctuation for this complete question.
questions.grammar_rule: A direct interrogative sentence normally ends with a question mark.
questions.example_sentence: When does the bus arrive?

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly for one teacher?
explanations: “Teachers” is a plural noun or bare form, not the singular possessive teacher’s.
“The teacher’s desk is tidy.” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Singular teacher takes apostrophe s to show possession.
“Teachers’” is the possessive of plural teachers, not one teacher.
questions.grammar_rule: Singular teacher takes apostrophe s to show possession.
questions.example_sentence: The teacher's bag is blue.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence with correct dialogue punctuation.
explanations: ““Come here,” she said.” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. In standard US punctuation, the comma belongs inside the closing quotation mark.
For this convention, the comma belongs inside the closing quotation mark, not after it.
The reporting clause follows a quoted command that requires the separating comma.
questions.grammar_rule: In standard US punctuation, the comma belongs inside the closing quotation mark.
questions.example_sentence: “Please wait,” she said.

questions.prompt: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: She does not knows the answer.
She does not know the answer.
She do not know the answer.
explanations: Knows wrongly adds -s after does, which already carries the agreement marking.
Know is the base form required after does not.
Do does not agree with the third-person singular subject she.
questions.grammar_rule: After does, use the base form of the main verb.
questions.example_sentence: He does not work on Sundays.

questions.prompt: Choose the standard comparative sentence.
options: This box is more heavier than that one.
This box is heavy than that one.
This box is heavier than that one.
explanations: More heavier doubles the comparative marking.
Heavy is the positive form and does not correctly combine with than here.
Heavier is the correct comparative form of heavy before than.
questions.grammar_rule: Do not combine more with the -er comparative form of the same adjective.
questions.example_sentence: This road is narrower than the other road.

questions.prompt: Correct the sentence “There is many reasons.”
explanations: “There are many reasons.” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Plural reasons requires there are.
“There is” does not agree with plural reasons, and “many reason” also lacks plural -s.
“There be” is not the correct finite form in this declarative sentence.
questions.grammar_rule: Plural reasons requires there are.
questions.example_sentence: There are many reasons to practise.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
explanations: “An advice” wrongly treats uncountable advice as a singular countable item.
“He gave me some advice.” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Advice is uncountable in standard English.
“Advices” is not the ordinary plural form of the uncountable noun advice.
questions.grammar_rule: Advice is uncountable in standard English.
questions.example_sentence: They have already finished their work.

questions.prompt: ___ had the speech begun when the microphone failed.
explanations: Hardly had ... when correctly expresses that the failure followed almost immediately.
Only does not form this fixed time-sequence construction.
Never had ... when does not fit the intended fixed construction.
questions.grammar_rule: Hardly had ... when introduces a past event quickly followed by another.
questions.example_sentence: Hardly had we arrived when it started raining.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct inversion after “Not until midnight”.
options: Not until midnight we reached home.
Not until midnight did we reach home.
Not until midnight we did reached home.
explanations: We reached keeps statement order after the fronted limiting phrase.
Did we reach uses correct auxiliary inversion and the base verb reach.
We did reached has incorrect order and wrongly places a past form after did.
questions.grammar_rule: A fronted negative/time-limiting expression can trigger auxiliary-subject inversion.
questions.example_sentence: Not until dawn did the storm stop.

questions.prompt: Had I known about the delay, I _____ earlier.
explanations: “would have left” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Had I known is an inverted third conditional equivalent to If I had known.
“Will leave” expresses a real future result rather than a contrary-to-fact past result.
“Had leaving” is ungrammatical and lacks the required past conditional result form.
questions.grammar_rule: Had I known is an inverted third conditional equivalent to If I had known.
questions.example_sentence: Had I known about the delay, I would have left earlier.

questions.prompt: Only after the meeting _____ the mistake.
explanations: “We noticed” omits the subject–auxiliary inversion triggered by initial “Only after”.
“did we notice” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. A fronted restrictive phrase Only after triggers subject–auxiliary inversion.
“Noticed we” inverts the main verb directly instead of using auxiliary did.
questions.grammar_rule: A fronted restrictive phrase Only after triggers subject–auxiliary inversion.
questions.example_sentence: Only after the meeting did we notice the mistake.

questions.prompt: At a hotel, the receptionist says: “Would you mind ___ this form?”
explanations: Complete is a bare infinitive and does not follow would you mind.
Completing is the gerund required after would you mind.
To complete is an infinitive, which is not normally used after would you mind.
questions.grammar_rule: Would you mind is followed by a gerund.
questions.example_sentence: Would you mind closing the window?

questions.prompt: A colleague says: “I will email the report as soon as I ___ it.”
explanations: Will finish is normally avoided within this future-time subordinate clause.
Finished would shift the clause into past time without an appropriate past-time frame.
Finish is the present simple used after as soon as for a future completion.
questions.grammar_rule: Future time clauses after as soon as usually use present simple for future reference.
questions.example_sentence: I will call you when I arrive.

questions.prompt: You missed a train yesterday. Which sentence reports it correctly?
options: I have missed the train yesterday.
explanations: Present perfect does not normally occur with a finished-time adverb such as yesterday.
“I missed the train yesterday.” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. The finished time yesterday requires simple past.
Present simple does not locate the missed train in the completed past.
questions.grammar_rule: The finished time yesterday requires simple past.
questions.example_sentence: I missed the train yesterday.

questions.prompt: In an email, choose the correct formal sentence.
options: Please let me know if you require any further information.
Please letting me know if you requires information.
Please let me knowing if you require information.
explanations: “Please let me know if you require any further information.” fits the intended grammatical contrast here. Let is followed by an object and the bare infinitive know.
“Please letting” is not an imperative construction, and “you requires” has incorrect agreement.
“Let me knowing” is not grammatical; let takes the base verb know.
questions.grammar_rule: Let is followed by an object and the bare infinitive know.
questions.example_sentence: I would appreciate your response at your earliest convenience.

questions.prompt: Which word is an adjective in “A quiet library helps me focus”?
explanations: Correct: Quiet describes the noun library, so it functions as an adjective.
Library is a noun naming a place, not a word that describes one.
Focus is a verb naming the act of concentrating, not an adjective.
questions.grammar_rule: Quiet describes the noun library, so it functions as an adjective.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: In “They arrived early,” which word is an adverb?
explanations: They is a subject pronoun referring to people, not an adverb.
Arrived is the past-tense action verb, not a word modifying that action.
Correct: Early modifies the verb arrived by telling us when they arrived.
questions.grammar_rule: Early modifies the verb arrived by telling us when they arrived.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: In “The train stopped suddenly,” which word expresses an action?
explanations: Train names a thing and is a noun.
Stopped tells what the train did and is a verb.
Suddenly modifies the stopping and is an adverb.
questions.grammar_rule: A verb tells what the subject does.
questions.example_sentence: The clock ticked loudly.

questions.prompt: In “Her kindness impressed us,” what part of speech is kindness?
explanations: Kindness names a quality and functions as a noun.
An adjective would describe a noun, but kindness is the noun itself.
A pronoun replaces a noun; kindness does not replace one.
questions.grammar_rule: An abstract noun names a quality or idea.
questions.example_sentence: Patience is valuable.

questions.prompt: Which is the plural of “mouse” when referring to animals?
explanations: Mouses is not the standard animal plural of mouse.
Correct: The irregular plural of mouse is mice.
Mousees incorrectly adds -es instead of using the irregular plural mice.
questions.grammar_rule: The irregular plural of mouse is mice.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the uncountable noun equipment correctly?
explanations: Equipment is uncountable and does not normally take the plural -s.
Equipment is singular in form, so the verb should be is, not are.
Correct: Equipment is uncountable and takes a singular verb.
questions.grammar_rule: Equipment is uncountable and takes a singular verb.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: Two _____ were grazing near the fence.
explanations: Sheeps is not the standard plural of sheep.
Sheep is correct after the number two.
Sheepes is not an English plural form.
questions.grammar_rule: Sheep has the same singular and plural form.
questions.example_sentence: Three deer crossed the road.

questions.prompt: Which phrase correctly shows that one teacher owns two books?
explanations: Teacher’s shows one teacher owns the books.
Book’s wrongly makes book possessive, and teachers lacks its marker.
Teachers’ means multiple teachers own the books.
questions.grammar_rule: Add apostrophe s to a singular possessor.
questions.example_sentence: The driver’s keys are here.

questions.prompt: Lina and I are ready. The guide will meet _____.
explanations: We is a subject pronoun; after meet the object form us is needed.
Correct: After the verb meet, use the object pronoun us.
Our is a possessive determiner and needs a following noun.
questions.grammar_rule: After the verb meet, use the object pronoun us.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: Each student must submit _____ own form.
explanations: Correct: Singular they/their is a natural gender-neutral way to refer to each student.
Them is an object pronoun, not a determiner before own form.
They is a subject pronoun and cannot modify own form here.
questions.grammar_rule: Singular they/their is a natural gender-neutral way to refer to each student.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: Please give the parcel to _____.
explanations: I is a subject pronoun, not the object of to.
Mine indicates possession and cannot name the recipient here.
Me is the object pronoun required after to.
questions.grammar_rule: Use an object pronoun after a preposition.
questions.example_sentence: The note is for her.

questions.prompt: Neither sister blamed _____ for the mistake.
explanations: Herself refers back to the sister who did the blaming.
Her would normally name someone else rather than refer back to the subject.
She is a subject pronoun and cannot be the direct object.
questions.grammar_rule: A reflexive pronoun refers back to the same subject.
questions.example_sentence: He reminded himself to call.

questions.prompt: She works at _____ university near the river.
explanations: An is used before vowel sounds; university starts with the consonant sound /j/.
Correct: University starts with a consonant /y/ sound, so use a.
The only would require an explicitly unique university and changes the intended indefinite meaning.
questions.grammar_rule: University starts with a consonant /y/ sound, so use a.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: We waited for _____ hour.
explanations: A does not fit the vowel sound at the start of hour because h is silent.
Correct: Hour begins with a vowel sound because h is silent.
Some cannot normally modify the singular countable noun hour in this construction.
questions.grammar_rule: Hour begins with a vowel sound because h is silent.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: They adopted _____ honest approach to the problem.
explanations: A is wrong because honest begins with a vowel sound.
An fits the initial vowel sound in honest.
A singular countable approach needs a determiner here.
questions.grammar_rule: Use an before a vowel sound, including silent h.
questions.example_sentence: It was an honour to meet you.

questions.prompt: _____ Pacific Ocean is larger than the Atlantic Ocean.
explanations: The is standard before Pacific Ocean.
An cannot introduce this proper ocean name.
A cannot replace the definite article for a named ocean.
questions.grammar_rule: Use the before the names of oceans.
questions.example_sentence: The Indian Ocean borders several countries.

questions.prompt: Of the three routes, this one is the _____.
explanations: Short is the positive degree and does not express the maximum among three.
Shorter is comparative for two; the superlative shortest is required among three.
Correct: Use the superlative shortest to compare three routes.
questions.grammar_rule: Use the superlative shortest to compare three routes.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: This box is _____ than the other one.
explanations: Heavy is the base adjective and does not express comparison with another box.
Correct: The comparative form of heavy is heavier.
Heaviest is superlative, but the sentence compares just two boxes.
questions.grammar_rule: The comparative form of heavy is heavier.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: This is the _____ solution of the two.
explanations: Simplest is superlative, normally used for three or more options.
More simplest combines a comparative marker with a superlative ending; it is not a grammatical comparative.
Simpler is the conventional comparative form of simple for two options.
questions.grammar_rule: Use the comparative when comparing two alternatives.
questions.example_sentence: Of these two bags, this one is lighter.

questions.prompt: After the storm, the streets looked _____.
explanations: Clean describes the streets after looked.
Cleanly is an adverb and does not describe the subject here.
Cleanliness is a noun, not the adjective required after looked.
questions.grammar_rule: A linking verb such as look takes a subject complement adjective.
questions.example_sentence: The garden looks beautiful.

questions.prompt: The baby slept _____.
explanations: Peaceful is an adjective; the action slept needs an adverb.
Correct: Peacefully is an adverb modifying slept.
Peace is a noun, not a manner adverb describing sleep.
questions.grammar_rule: Peacefully is an adverb modifying slept.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: I _____ visit my grandparents on Sundays.
explanations: Usual is an adjective, whereas visit needs a frequency adverb.
Correct: Usually is a frequency adverb used with visit.
Usualness is a noun and cannot modify the verb visit in this position.
questions.grammar_rule: Usually is a frequency adverb used with visit.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: We have _____ completed the final review.
explanations: Yet is usual in negative sentences or questions, not this affirmative position.
Already naturally indicates completion by now.
Ever commonly asks about experience; it does not indicate completion here.
questions.grammar_rule: Already commonly marks completion earlier than expected.
questions.example_sentence: I have already sent the email.

questions.prompt: She answered the question _____.
explanations: Confidently modifies answered and tells how she answered.
Confident is an adjective; it cannot directly modify answered.
Confidence is a noun, not a manner adverb.
questions.grammar_rule: Use an adverb to modify how an action is performed.
questions.example_sentence: He explained the rules clearly.

questions.prompt: Our class begins _____ nine o’clock.
explanations: Correct: At introduces an exact clock time.
On is used for days and dates, not a precise clock time.
In is commonly used for months, years and broad periods, not nine o’clock.
questions.grammar_rule: At introduces an exact clock time.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: The appointment is _____ Monday.
explanations: In does not introduce a day of the week in this time expression.
At is used for specific times, but not normally before Monday.
Correct: On is used with named days.
questions.grammar_rule: On is used with named days.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: He has worked here _____ 2019.
explanations: For introduces a duration such as five years, not a year as the starting point here.
Since correctly identifies when the employment began.
During introduces a period or event, not this continuing starting point.
questions.grammar_rule: Since introduces a starting point in time.
questions.example_sentence: They have been friends since childhood.

questions.prompt: The cat ran _____ the room and hid under a chair.
explanations: Into shows the cat entered the room.
Onto describes movement to a surface, not entry into an enclosed space.
Across of is not a grammatical prepositional phrase.
questions.grammar_rule: Into describes movement from outside to inside.
questions.example_sentence: She walked into the kitchen.

questions.prompt: It was raining, _____ we stayed indoors.
explanations: But would signal an unexpected contrast rather than the result of the rain.
Correct: So joins the cause and its result.
Although normally introduces a subordinate clause and cannot join these clauses in this position.
questions.grammar_rule: So joins the cause and its result.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: _____ she was tired, she finished the report.
explanations: Correct: Although introduces a contrasting subordinate clause.
Because of takes a noun phrase or gerund, not the complete clause she was tired.
Unless means except if and does not express the intended contrast.
questions.grammar_rule: Although introduces a contrasting subordinate clause.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: I will call you _____ I reach the airport.
explanations: Unless introduces an exception, changing the intended timing.
When correctly marks the arrival time.
Despite is a preposition and cannot introduce this finite clause alone.
questions.grammar_rule: When introduces the time a future action happens.
questions.example_sentence: I will text you when I arrive.

questions.prompt: He saved his notes _____ he could revise them later.
explanations: So that links saving notes to the purpose of later revision.
Although signals contrast, not the intended purpose.
Whereas expresses contrast between clauses, not purpose.
questions.grammar_rule: So that introduces purpose or intended result.
questions.example_sentence: I left early so that I could catch the train.

questions.prompt: Listen! Someone _____ at the door.
explanations: Knocks could describe a habit, but Listen! signals an action occurring right now.
Correct: Present continuous describes an action happening right now.
Knocked is past simple, inconsistent with the current event indicated by Listen!.
questions.grammar_rule: Present continuous describes an action happening right now.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: Nadia _____ to school by bus every day.
explanations: Go lacks the -es required with a third-person singular subject in the present simple.
Going needs an auxiliary such as is and does not form a finite main verb alone.
Correct: Third-person singular Nadia takes goes in the simple present.
questions.grammar_rule: Third-person singular Nadia takes goes in the simple present.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: The librarian _____ the doors at nine every weekday.
explanations: Open lacks -s with the singular subject librarian.
Opens is appropriate for a repeated weekday schedule.
Is opening yesterday combines present ongoing tense with a past-time marker.
questions.grammar_rule: Third-person singular habitual actions use simple present -s.
questions.example_sentence: My neighbour walks to work daily.

questions.prompt: I _____ for my keys all morning, and I still cannot find them.
explanations: Have been looking expresses ongoing searching until now.
Looked yesterday refers to a distinct finished past time.
Am look is not a grammatical verb phrase.
questions.grammar_rule: Present perfect continuous links a continuing activity with now.
questions.example_sentence: She has been studying since breakfast.

questions.prompt: Yesterday we _____ the museum.
explanations: Visit is not past tense and conflicts with the completed-time marker yesterday.
Correct: Yesterday indicates a completed past action, so use visited.
Visiting is a participle needing an auxiliary; it cannot stand as the main finite verb here.
questions.grammar_rule: Yesterday indicates a completed past action, so use visited.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: While I _____, the phone rang.
explanations: Correct: Past continuous shows an ongoing action interrupted by another past event.
Cooked always is not a natural form for an action underway when the phone rang.
Have cooked links a past action to the present, not an action interrupted in the past.
questions.grammar_rule: Past continuous shows an ongoing action interrupted by another past event.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: When the lights went out, we _____ dinner.
explanations: Have eaten is present perfect and does not express the action in progress then.
Were eating describes an ongoing past activity at the moment the lights failed.
Eat tomorrow is not a grammatical past-tense completion here.
questions.grammar_rule: Past continuous shows an ongoing event interrupted in the past.
questions.example_sentence: I was reading when the alarm rang.

questions.prompt: She _____ her passport before she left for the airport.
explanations: Had checked locates the checking before she left.
Has check is ungrammatical because has needs the participle checked.
Checks tomorrow does not agree with the past sequence.
questions.grammar_rule: Past perfect marks an event before another past event.
questions.example_sentence: He had locked the door before he departed.

questions.prompt: Look at those dark clouds. It _____ rain.
explanations: Correct: Going to is used for predictions based on visible evidence.
Was is incomplete before rain and does not express this evidence-based future prediction.
Has rain is ungrammatical; has would need a past participle, and the context predicts the future.
questions.grammar_rule: Going to is used for predictions based on visible evidence.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: I think the team _____ win tomorrow.
explanations: Correct: Will naturally expresses an opinion-based future prediction.
Was win is not a grammatical verb phrase and fails the future prediction.
Have win uses the wrong auxiliary and verb form for a future prediction.
questions.grammar_rule: Will naturally expresses an opinion-based future prediction.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: At 8 p.m. tomorrow, I _____ for my exam.
explanations: Will have studied yesterday mixes future perfect with a past-time marker.
Will be studying shows the action ongoing at 8 p.m. tomorrow.
Study last night has a past marker without a past verb.
questions.grammar_rule: Future continuous describes an action in progress at a stated future time.
questions.example_sentence: At noon tomorrow, we will be travelling.

questions.prompt: The phone is ringing; I _____ it.
explanations: Will answer expresses a decision made now.
Answered yesterday is a past event, not a current response.
Have answering is an invalid verb construction.
questions.grammar_rule: Will is commonly used for an immediate decision.
questions.example_sentence: I will get the door.

questions.prompt: She said she _____ busy the following day.
explanations: Is keeps a present-time perspective instead of the ordinary past-reporting backshift requested.
Correct: Would be is a natural future-in-the-past form after said.
Will be yesterday combines future modal wording with a past-time adverb and is ungrammatical.
questions.grammar_rule: Would be is a natural future-in-the-past form after said.
questions.example_sentence: Independent grammar example required before approval.

questions.prompt: By the time we arrived, the guests _____ dinner.
